heading: Before there were area codes
paragraphs: Before you could tap a name on your phone and hear someone's voice, making a call meant turning a dial.

On a rotary phone, you placed your finger in the hole beside a number and pulled the dial around until it stopped. Then you let go. As the dial spun back, it sent a series of electrical pulses down the telephone line. Dial a 3, and it sent three pulses. Dial a 7, and it sent seven. Zero was the exception: it sent ten.
These pulses were how the telephone network understood the number you were calling.

As the telephone system grew, connecting calls between different parts of the country became more complicated. The solution was a national numbering plan. In 1947, AT&T assigned area codes to geographic territories across the United States and Canada.
An area code was the first part of a telephone number. It told the switching equipment where a call needed to go before the rest of the number directed it to a local exchange.
But there was something unusual about the original system: area codes took different amounts of time to dial.
A code like 212, assigned to New York City, took just five pulses. A code like 605, assigned to South Dakota, took 21.
That difference is the starting point for this map.

The usual explanation is that the busiest places received the shortest codes, saving time on millions of calls. The pattern is visible in the data, although the reason for the original assignments is disputed.
What follows is a map of that original numbering plan, measured in the clicks it took to make a call.
